rv.q: Tharp's achievement here, and it is a brilliant achievement

A sleek, energizing mixture of Sinatra’s inimitable cool and Ms. Tharp’s kinetic heat, “Away” sweeps you up in a spell so complete that only those resistant to the seductions of dance or the swing of Sinatra will be left on the other side of the velvet rope.
But there's nothing superfluous about Away, choreographed and directed by Twyla Tharp.
Twyla Tharp's Away is not just the best date show on Broadway; it's a bit like being on a great date yourself.
The super-cool song stylings of Frank Sinatra have been given an additional layer of sexiness in "Away," Twyla Tharp's libido-charged love letter to romance, not to mention the man and his music.

"Away," Tharp's dangerously gorgeous, wordless dance adventure, asks audiences to put aside the usual expectations of plot and to follow the delicious and foolish complexities of four relationships through exhilarating, scary-smart movement.
The downside is that, after a while, repetitiveness seeps in.
The show will best be appreciated by dance aficionados rather than general audiences, who might be put off by the lack of a coherent story line.
“Away” seems unlikely to grab repeat customers the way “Movin’ Out” did.

The show succeeds brilliantly as pure entertainment, featuring gorgeous dancing and staging that makes you feel like you're in a classic nightclub.
Twyla Tharp is back on her A game, this time with Frank Sinatra as a collaborator.
Though the individual numbers are thrilling and brilliantly executed, the total experience is less engaging than one would expect.

Tharp finds inspiration even in Sinatra's less-stellar material: That old chestnut New York, New York becomes an exuberant finale — a fitting end to a show that, though less than the sum of its glorious parts, is buoyed by its subject's inimitable spirit.
We are duly tickled, fascinated and stunned by what we see, but almost never moved.
Tharp's latest can be as tedious as waiting on a tarmac.

Fly me to the moon Let me play among the stars Let me see what spring is like On Jupiter and Mars Bart Howard's words are as good as any to conjure the euphoric, elating spirit of Twyla Tharp's newest contribution to Broadway.
Their energy is high and they really heat up the joint.
By using Sinatra merely for decorative mood music, "Away" lacks the raw passion and youthful energy that made "Movin' Out' so stunning.
